source.basis: Operator facility page; structured facts only, no operator prose reproduced.

reading.body:
EdgeCore Ashburn AS01 publishes 114 MW of IT capacity, the third largest figure among Virginia data centers that disclose one, but not where that power comes from.

The facility covers 685,000 square feet in Sterling, Virginia. At 40 kW per rack, a common AI training density, 114 MW implies roughly 2,850 racks, though the operator does not specify workload mix or tenant configuration. Virginia's 25 facilities with published megawatt figures total 1,603 MW, so this one campus accounts for 7.1 percent of the state's disclosed IT load. The state maps 330 facilities, which means most publish no capacity at all. Disclosure, not construction, is the scarce thing.

For AI, published megawatts are the closest available proxy for how much compute a building can hold. A 114 MW campus sits in the tier that matters for training clusters, and rack density determines whether that power becomes accelerators or ordinary servers. But the number describes an envelope, not a workload. What fills it is not stated.

What the data does not cover is the part that decides whether the campus can run. There is no power source, no grid connection point, no indication of whether supply comes from existing utility capacity or new generation, and no statement of whether the full 114 MW is allocated or available. LEED certification speaks to building efficiency, not to where the electricity comes from. Without those facts, the facility's place in Virginia's power constraint cannot be judged, only its size.
